subject: history
title: Plantations & the Slave Trade Adventure
welcome_lead: Britain's empire was built partly on a terrible business — the transatlantic slave trade and the plantations it served.
meta_desc: Plantations Adventure — a KS3 History walkthrough of how the British Empire used slavery on Caribbean plantations.
final_note: You learned how the triangle trade worked, what life on a plantation was like, and how Britain grew rich from enslaved labour.

walkthroughs.body_html:
From the 1600s to the early 1800s British ships took part in a three-leg triangle trade.

  • Leg 1: Europe → Africa, carrying guns, cloth and beads.
  • Leg 2: Africa → the Americas, carrying enslaved Africans.
  • Leg 3: Americas → Europe, carrying sugar, tobacco and cotton.

The middle leg was the Middle Passage — a horrific journey on packed slave ships. Many died on the way. ⚓

In the Caribbean (Jamaica, Barbados) enslaved Africans worked on huge sugar plantations.

They worked from dawn till dusk in the heat, cutting and crushing sugar cane. They were whipped, branded, badly fed and could be bought and sold.

Families were broken up. Resistance — running away or revolting — was punished with death.

Slavery was a key part of British wealth in the 1700s.

Ports like Bristol, Liverpool and Glasgow grew rich building and supplying slave ships. Plantation owners bought big country houses in Britain.

Sugar in tea, cotton for cloth, tobacco for pipes — many British comforts came from enslaved labour. 💰

mcqs.q: Why is Magna Carta still cited in 'Power and the People' history?
options: Wannsee was the meeting where Hitler personally launched WWII.
Magna Carta directly created modern human rights in 1215.
Because clauses on lawful judgement and protection from arbitrary imprisonment were reinterpreted in the 17th century to support broader liberties, even though they originally protected only barons.
Magna Carta gave the right to vote to all English men.

Wannsee was the meeting where Hitler personally launched WWII.
Drake defeated the Armada single-handedly in a great sea battle.
